profiles.meeting_scenario: Two coauthors of a newly finished systematic survey on deep reinforcement learning for recommender systems meet to brainstorm a concrete follow-up research direction that could become both a workshop paper and the survey's 'future directions' companion project. The context is that they have just synthesized the literature and now want to turn broad observations into 2-3 candidate projects that feel timely, tractable, and publishable. The agenda is to identify promising gaps from the survey, discuss what kind of benchmark or study would make the gap actionable, and loosely align on a short list of next steps. The expected outcome is not a final project plan, but an apparently shared picture of one leading idea: a benchmark-oriented study on DRL for recommender systems that addresses cold-start and long-term evaluation in a more realistic setting.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: Sequential recommendation, offline evaluation, reproducible benchmarking in academic ML
members.background: Former ranking scientist at a large e-commerce platform, now runs a university lab focused on recommendation evaluation and dataset curation; she led the systematic review and wants a follow-up project that can be executed by students with public resources.
members.private_state: She wants a follow-up idea that is publishable within one semester, uses public datasets, and strengthens her lab's reputation for careful benchmarking rather than ambitious platform-building.
hidden_assumptions: When recommender-system papers mention 'cold-start' without qualification, they usually mean new-user cold-start.
A 'benchmark' follow-up to a survey should primarily mean standardized preprocessing, task definitions, and evaluation scripts on public logged datasets.
For a future-directions paper to be credible, gains should replicate across multiple public datasets rather than rely on a single complex environment.
When someone casually references 'the Kuaishou dataset' in DRL recommender discussions, they most likely mean KuaiRec because it is the canonical public benchmark she has in mind from the survey.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.role: Senior PhD student and survey coauthor
members.expertise: Reinforcement learning, user simulation, long-horizon recommendation under delayed feedback
members.background: Final-year PhD student who previously interned on short-video recommendation systems and has been pushing simulator-based evaluation for RL methods; he sees the survey as a launchpad for a thesis chapter on interactive benchmarking.
members.private_state: He wants the brainstorming session to drift toward an ambitious simulator-backed benchmark that showcases long-term reward and feels relevant to industry labs evaluating retention rather than just clicks.
hidden_assumptions: In creator-feed and content-platform discussions, 'cold-start' naturally refers to new-item or new-creator exposure rather than new users.
A benchmark is only truly useful for DRL if it includes some interactive component, such as a learned user simulator or closed-loop rollout environment.
A result can count as strong evidence even if it appears in one especially realistic environment, as long as that environment exposes long-term trade-offs hidden by standard offline setups.
When people mention 'the Kuaishou data' in this subfield, they often mean KuaiRand-style logged interaction data from the short-video line of work rather than KuaiRec specifically.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'cold-start' means in the follow-up idea
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the project should cover 'cold-start in DRL recommenders.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means new-user cold-start: the challenge is making long-term recommendation policies work when a user has little or no interaction history.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means new-item/new-creator cold-start: the challenge is how a DRL policy explores and allocates exposure to fresh content over time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because 'cold-start' is a standard umbrella term in recommender systems, each assumes the other is using the conventional meaning from their own subcommunity and the phrase sounds fully aligned on the surface.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'benchmark' for the project
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should build a 'lightweight benchmark' as the concrete follow-up.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a compact benchmark package around existing public datasets: curated splits, standardized state/action formatting, and evaluation scripts that others can run offline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a still-manageable but interactive benchmark suite: public logs plus a learned user simulator and rollout API so DRL methods can be tested in closed loop.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The adjective 'lightweight' feels reassuring to both of them, but each silently treats a different boundary as obvious—M1 focuses on implementation burden, while M2 focuses on avoiding full production infrastructure.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the project needs 'convincing evidence' that DRL helps in recommendation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks convincing means stable, reproducible improvements across several public datasets and task variants, even if the gains are modest.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks convincing means demonstrating a clear long-term benefit in at least one realistic interactive environment, even if standard offline datasets show mixed or weak results.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither person thinks they are disagreeing about standards because both invoke the same high-level quality language; the divergence only appears in what each person imagines as sufficient proof.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'Kuaishou dataset' they have in mind
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both casually propose including 'the Kuaishou dataset' among the benchmark resources.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is picturing KuaiRec, the fully observed recommendation dataset she associates with reproducible public benchmarking.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is picturing KuaiRand, the logged short-video interaction dataset he associates with more realistic policy-learning behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The datasets come from the same research lineage and are often referred to informally by platform name, so each hears a familiar reference and sees no need to disambiguate in a fast brainstorming meeting.

turns.inner_thought: The survey will read stronger if we pair it with one concrete, executable artifact. I really do not want us to drift into three half-baked future-work bullets that require infrastructure no student can maintain. The safest path is a benchmark package around public datasets, with clearly defined preprocessing, task splits, baselines, and scripts that can be wrapped up in a semester.
turns.utterance: Now that the survey is basically done, I think the future-directions piece should probably collapse into one concrete benchmark-oriented follow-up rather than a grab bag of speculative ideas. If we can make it focused and reusable, that would give the survey a much cleaner afterlife.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's open to a benchmark. If we center it on cold-start, we can naturally motivate interactive evaluation, since new creators and fresh content only really make sense when the policy has to trade short-term engagement against longer-term ecosystem health. For me the real win is showing long-horizon value, even if it comes through most clearly in one realistic environment.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I like that. One gap that keeps standing out to me is cold-start, because that's where DRL should matter most if we care about more than immediate clicks. It gives us a believable reason to talk about long-term behavior instead of just re-running standard ranking baselines.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly: new-user cold-start is a nice fit for an academic benchmark. We can create standardized histories, sparse-profile conditions, and common state/action interfaces on public logs. Students can run it without special infrastructure, and we can compare offline RL or bandit-style methods in a controlled way across multiple datasets.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We could make that actionable by building a lightweight benchmark around cold-start recommendation, using public datasets and a standardized state/action interface so people are not all implementing slightly different task definitions. That feels concrete enough for a workshop paper.

turns.inner_thought: She said lightweight benchmark, which is perfect if I frame the simulator as minimal and manageable. We don't need production complexity, just enough of an interactive loop that rollout effects appear. Otherwise people will claim to study DRL but still evaluate in a static offline way that hides the retention trade-offs I care about.
turns.utterance: That sounds right to me. I think the lightweight benchmark would be especially compelling if there were at least some interactive loop in it, so the long-horizon effects can actually show up rather than getting flattened into one-step metrics. Even a modest closed-loop component could make the story much sharper.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with a small interactive component as long as the core remains a clean public benchmark package. We should definitely include KuaiRec, since that's the obvious Kuaishou dataset for reproducible benchmarking, and then maybe one or two other public datasets so any pattern isn't dataset-specific. Replication across datasets is what will make the evidence credible.
turns.utterance: We could probably include the Kuaishou dataset alongside one or two other public resources and then look for patterns that replicate cleanly. If the setup is consistent across them, that already gives us a strong narrative about what transfers and what doesn't.

turns.inner_thought: Great, she also wants Kuaishou data. KuaiRand would be ideal for short-video dynamics and multi-step exposure effects, especially for creator-side exploration under cold-start. That's exactly the kind of setting where an interactive prototype would feel grounded rather than toyish.
turns.utterance: Yes, the Kuaishou data would be a really good anchor here. It should let us test whether the policy handles cold-start over multiple recommendation steps, which is where a lot of the interesting behavior actually emerges.

turns.inner_thought: We're aligned: keep the pipeline clean, avoid overengineering, and see whether the same basic result appears on several public datasets. If we can show stable effects across different benchmark resources with shared preprocessing and evaluation, that's the kind of careful evidence my lab should be known for.
turns.utterance: And the nice part is that, if we keep the setup clean enough, convincing evidence should come from seeing the same basic effect across datasets without overengineering the pipeline. I would much rather have a result people can reproduce easily than something flashy but fragile.

turns.inner_thought: I agree on rigor, but I don't want us to over-index on needing broad replication if one realistic environment already exposes the long-term advantage. In this area, static benchmarks often miss the point. If the simulator-backed setting reveals retention gains clearly, that can be the centerpiece even if the ordinary offline results are mixed.
turns.utterance: Totally, though I also think even one realistic environment could be convincing if it reveals long-term retention gains that ordinary offline recommendation benchmarks tend to wash out. Sometimes the whole issue is that the standard setup is too myopic to surface the effect we care about.

turns.inner_thought: I should steer this toward something academics can actually pick up quickly. The framing should be: here is an accessible benchmark for studying cold-start in DRL recommenders, with public resources and minimal engineering burden. That keeps it publishable soon and useful for the community.
turns.utterance: I think the framing should really emphasize practical entry points for academics. If the benchmark is easy for other groups to reuse when studying cold-start DRL, that alone makes it valuable, because right now everyone has to reconstruct the setup from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll draft the environment side around a Kuaishou-based prototype—ideally something simulator-backed from the short-video logs—and let Lina handle the benchmark framing from the survey. If I get a decent rollout API working, I can nudge the project toward the interactive thesis chapter I want.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Why don't I sketch the environment side and put together a Kuaishou-based prototype, and you can draft the benchmark framing and the broader motivation coming out of the survey? Then next week we can see whether the pieces line up into one leading story.
